title: S3Bio Lab Orientation
text:
Welcome
Welcome to the Systems.Synthetic.Systematic Biology (S3Bio) lab! We are thrilled to have you join our team.
This orientation book is designed to help you navigate your first few weeks in the lab.






NoteFirst Steps




Complete your safety training.
Set up your lab accounts.
Schedule a meeting with your mentor.

title: 1  About S3Bio Lab
text:
1.1 Our Philosophy
The Systems.Synthetic.Systematic Biology (S3Bio) lab focuses on three core pillars:
We believe in open science, collaboration, and systematic rigor. Every member of our lab contributes to a culture of innovation and respect.

title: 2  Onboarding: Getting Started
text:
2.1 General Setup (All Members)
Welcome to your first week! Here’s a checklist of things to get set up.

title: 2  Onboarding: Getting Started
text:
Email & Identity: Got your university email from the University.
Lab Access: Request a face recognition access from the department administrator.
MS Teams: Join the #S3Bio channel at S3Bio MS Teams.
Emergency Contact: Fill out the lab’s emergency contact form.

title: 2  Onboarding: Getting Started
text:
2.2 Safety Training & Acknowledgment (All Members)

Personal Protection: Read and understand PPE Requirements.
Lab Regulations: Read and understand General Lab Regulations.
Code of Conduct: Review and sign the Lab Code of Conduct.
Data Policy: Review and sign the Data Management Policy.

title: 2  Onboarding: Getting Started
text:
2.3 Specific Onboarding
Please follow the checklist for your specific role:

Wet Lab MembersDry Lab Members



Biosafety: Read Biosafety Protocols and complete university BSL-2 training.
Chemical Safety: Read Chemical Safety and locate all SDS for your project.
Waste Management: Read Waste Management and identify all waste collection points.
Safety Tour: Complete the in-person wet lab safety walkthrough with your advisor.
Chemical Inventory: Get access to the lab’s chemical tracking system with your advisor.
Equipment Training: Schedule training for the equipment with your advisor.




Github Account: Create a GitHub account then send the username and email to your advisor.
Github Training: Study the lab’s GitHub workflow and best practices.
Code of Conduct: Review the lab’s code of conduct and data management policies.
Server Access: Request access to the high-performance computing (HPC) cluster from your advisor.
VPN Setup: Configure the university VPN for remote data access.










ImportantOnboarding Deadline



Please complete these tasks within your first month.

title: 3  Code of Conduct & Data Policies
text:
3.1 Code of Conduct
The S3Bio lab is committed to fostering a safe, inclusive, and professionally rigorous environment. All members are expected to adhere to our Code of Conduct and Data Management policies.
Our lab thrives on collaboration and mutual respect. We expect all members to:
crumbs: 3  Code of Conduct & Data Policies

title: 3  Code of Conduct & Data Policies
text:
Be Inclusive: Welcome and support people of all backgrounds and identities.
Be Considerate: Your work affects others. Communicate early and often about shared resources or equipment.
Be Professional: Use professional language and conduct in all lab-related communications, including Slack, GitHub, and email.
Academic Integrity: Maintain the highest standards of honesty in all research and publication activities. Plagiarism and data fabrication are strictly prohibited.
Reporting: If you experience or witness harassment or unprofessional behavior, please report it to the PI or the university’s ombudsperson.
crumbs: 3  Code of Conduct & Data Policies

title: 3  Code of Conduct & Data Policies
text:
3.2 Data Management Policy
In the S3Bio lab, data is our most valuable asset. Proper management ensures reproducibility and long-term utility.

3.2.1 Data Storage & Backup

Raw Data: Must be backed up immediately to the lab’s primary network-attached storage (NAS) or designated cloud provider. Never delete raw data.
Active Projects: Use the lab’s GitHub organization for code and small metadata. Large binaries should be managed via Git LFS or external links.
Personal Devices: Lab data should not be stored exclusively on personal laptops. Use the provided sync tools to ensure all work is backed up to lab servers.



3.2.2 Metadata & Documentation

Lab Notebooks: All members must maintain a digital lab notebook (e.g., Benchling, LabArchives, or a dedicated Markdown repo).
Data Dictionary: Every dataset must include a README or data dictionary explaining the variables, units, and collection methods.



3.2.3 Open Science & Sharing

Public Release: Upon publication, all relevant code and data must be made publicly available (e.g., via Zenodo, Figshare, or GitHub) unless restricted by IRB or privacy agreements.
Authorship: Authorship should be discussed early in a project and follow the CRediT (Contributor Roles Taxonomy) guidelines.







ImportantAcknowledgment



By working in the S3Bio lab, you agree to uphold these standards. Please sign the policy acknowledgment form during your first week.
crumbs: 3  Code of Conduct & Data Policies

title: 4  Lab Resources & Protocols
text:
4.1 Computing Resources
The S3Bio lab uses a wide range of tools and resources. This chapter provides a guide to our facilities and the standard protocols we follow.

title: 4  Lab Resources & Protocols
text:
GitHub: Our organization can be found at github.com/S3Bio. All code should be hosted here.
High-Performance Computing (HPC): We use the university’s cluster for large-scale simulations and data processing. See the Lab Manager for an account.
Shared Drive: Large datasets and administrative documents are stored on our lab NAS.
Zotero: We use a shared Zotero library for literature management.

title: 4  Lab Resources & Protocols
text:
4.2 Lab Equipment & Facilities

Molecular Biology Suite: Contains our PCR machines, gel electrophoresis equipment, and centrifuges.
Imaging Core: Houses our confocal and fluorescence microscopes. Booking must be done 24 hours in advance via the Booking Portal.
Tissue Culture Lab: Access requires specific Level 2 training.
Cold Storage:

-20°C: Common reagents and enzymes.
-80°C: Long-term sample storage. Every box must be clearly labeled and logged in the lab inventory.

title: 4  Lab Resources & Protocols
text:
4.3 Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs)
Following these protocols ensures consistency and safety in our research.

4.3.1 Sample Preparation

All biological samples must be labeled with: Date, Sample ID, and User Initials.
Use the designated “Clean Room” for high-sensitivity RNA work.



4.3.2 Data Acquisition

Naming Convention: All files should follow the YYYY-MM-DD_ProjectID_Description format.
Metadata: Every experiment must have a corresponding entry in the electronic lab notebook (ELN) detailing all experimental parameters.



4.3.3 Equipment Maintenance

Sign-in Logs: Always sign the logbook for the PCR and Imaging systems.
Reporting Faults: If a piece of equipment is malfunctioning, tag it “Out of Order” and notify the Lab Manager immediately.



4.3.4 Laboratory Hygiene

Bench Cleaning: Wipe down your workspace with 70% Ethanol before and after every session.
Waste Disposal:

Red Bins: Biohazardous waste.
Yellow Bins: Sharps.
Blue Bins: Non-hazardous glass.








NoteAccessing Full Protocols



A complete list of our detailed experimental protocols (e.g., Miniprep, NGS Library Prep, CRISPR Screen) can be found on our Internal Lab Wiki.

title: 5  Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
text:
5.1 Mandatory PPE
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is your first line of defense against laboratory hazards. In the S3Bio lab, wearing the correct PPE is mandatory at all times.
Whenever you are working at a lab bench, you must wear:

title: 5  Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
text:
Lab Coat: Must be buttoned and have long sleeves. Lab coats should stay in the lab and never be worn in common areas (breakrooms, offices).
Gloves: Nitrile gloves are standard. Change your gloves immediately if they become contaminated or torn. Never touch door handles or keyboards with gloved hands.
Eye Protection: Safety glasses or goggles must be worn when handling liquids, chemicals, or biological agents.

title: 5  Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
text:
5.2 Proper Attire
Beyond PPE, your general clothing must also provide protection:

Closed-toe Shoes: Sandals, flip-flops, and open-toed shoes are strictly prohibited in the lab.
Long Pants: Your legs must be fully covered. No shorts or skirts above the knee.
Hair & Jewelry: Tie back long hair and avoid dangling jewelry or loose clothing that could get caught in equipment.

title: 5  Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
text:
5.3 Hygiene

Hand Washing: Always wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water after removing your gloves and before leaving the lab.
No Food or Drink: Consumption of food or drink is strictly prohibited in all laboratory areas. Do not store food in lab refrigerators.







ImportantPPE Availability



If you need a new lab coat or specific types of gloves (e.g., for extreme cold or specific chemicals), contact the Lab Manager immediately.

title: 6  General Lab Regulations
text:
6.1 Professional Conduct
A safe and efficient lab environment is built on shared responsibility and adherence to clear regulations.

title: 6  General Lab Regulations
text:
No Lone Working: Avoid working in the lab alone, especially after hours or with hazardous materials. If you must, ensure the PI or a lab mate is aware and checks in on you periodically.
No Unauthorized Visitors: All visitors must be approved by the PI and receive a safety briefing before entering the lab.

title: 6  General Lab Regulations
text:
6.2 Workspace Management

Cleanliness: Keep your assigned bench space organized and clean. Clean up any spills (no matter how small) immediately.
Labelling: Every container, tube, and box must be clearly labeled with the contents, date, and your initials. Unlabeled containers will be discarded.
Shared Areas: Clean common equipment (e.g., balances, centrifuges, PCR machines) immediately after use.

title: 6  General Lab Regulations
text:
6.3 Emergency Preparedness

Know the Locations: Familiarize yourself with the location of the nearest:

Emergency Exit
First Aid Kit
Fire Extinguisher
Eyewash Station and Safety Shower

Incident Reporting: All accidents, near-misses, and chemical/biological spills must be reported to the PI and the University Safety Office within 24 hours.

title: 6  General Lab Regulations
text:
6.4 Off-Hours Access

Access Codes: Do not share your lab access code or keycard with anyone.
Secure the Lab: If you are the last person to leave, ensure all equipment is properly shut down (except for designated always-on machines), the lights are off, and the doors are securely locked.

title: 6  General Lab Regulations
text:
6.5 Sharps Waste

Sharps Containers: Dispose of all needles, scalpels, and other sharp objects in puncture-resistant, labeled sharps containers.
Never Recap Needles: Dispose of needles immediately after use without recapping.
Broken Glass: Use a designated “Broken Glass” box for non-contaminated broken glass. If the glass is contaminated with biological or chemical hazards, treat it appropriately before disposal.

title: 6  General Lab Regulations
text:
6.6 Regular Trash

No Hazards: Ensure that no biological, chemical, or sharps materials end up in the regular trash or recycling bins.
Cleanliness: Keep the trash areas tidy and do not block access to waste containers.







NoteSafety Contact Information



Emergency contact numbers (PI, Lab Manager, Security) are posted by the main lab entrance.

title: 7  Biosafety Protocols
text:
7.1 Biosafety Levels (BSL)
The S3Bio lab handles a variety of biological materials, including bacteria, cell lines, and viral vectors. Adherence to biosafety protocols is essential to protect yourself and the environment.
Our lab is classified for BSL-2 work.

title: 7  Biosafety Protocols
text:
BSL-1: For agents not known to cause disease in healthy adults (e.g., E. coli K-12).
BSL-2: For agents associated with human disease (e.g., specific cell lines, viral vectors). Access is restricted, and specialized PPE and containment are required.

title: 7  Biosafety Protocols
text:
7.2 Biological Safety Cabinet (BSC) Usage

Pre-work: Surface-decontaminate the BSC with 70% ethanol before starting work.
Work Practices: Keep the air intake grill clear. Work at least 6 inches back from the front opening.
Aseptic Technique: Use proper aseptic techniques to prevent contamination of your samples and the lab environment.
Post-work: Decontaminate the BSC and run the UV light for the required time (usually 15-20 minutes).

title: 7  Biosafety Protocols
text:
7.3 Storage and Transport

Secondary Containment: Use leak-proof, shatterproof secondary containers when transporting biological materials between labs or to and from cold storage.
Labeling: Ensure all biological samples are clearly labeled with the agent name, date, and BSL level.

title: 7  Biosafety Protocols
text:
7.4 Decontamination and Spills

Surface Decontamination: Wipe down all work surfaces with a freshly prepared 10% bleach solution or 70% ethanol after every experimental session.
Biohazard Spills: In case of a biological spill:

Alert others and evacuate the area if needed.
Wait 30 minutes for aerosols to settle.
Follow the established spill cleanup procedure using the biohazard spill kit.








WarningTraining Requirement



You must complete the university’s online and in-person biosafety training before beginning any BSL-2 work.

title: 8  Chemical Safety
text:
8.1 Safety Data Sheets (SDS)
Chemical safety in the S3Bio lab depends on your knowledge of the materials you use and proper handling techniques.
Every chemical in the lab has a corresponding SDS. Before using a new chemical: - Review the SDS: Understand the hazards, PPE requirements, and emergency procedures. - Know the Symbols: Be familiar with the GHS hazard symbols (e.g., flammable, corrosive, toxic).

title: 8  Chemical Safety
text:
8.2 Proper Storage

Compatibility: Store chemicals in compatible groups. Never store acids with bases or flammables with oxidizers.
Storage Cabinets:

Flammable Cabinets: For all flammable liquids.
Acid/Base Cabinets: For corrosive materials.

Secondary Containment: Use trays to catch any potential leaks or spills in storage.

title: 8  Chemical Safety
text:
8.3 Fume Hood Usage
Use the fume hood when working with volatile, toxic, or odorous chemicals.

Check the Airflow: Verify the fume hood is operational before starting work.
Keep it Clear: Don’t clutter the hood with storage. Keep items at least 6 inches from the front sash.
Sash Height: Keep the sash at or below the designated safe working level.

title: 8  Chemical Safety
text:
8.4 Key Rules

Label Everything: Even common reagents (like 70% EtOH) must be clearly labeled with the name, concentration, and date.
No Mouth Pipetting: Always use a mechanical pipetting device.
Transport Carefully: Use a bottle carrier when moving glass bottles of chemicals.
Never Mix Concentrated Acids with Water: Always add acid to water slowly, with stirring.







ImportantChemical Inventory



Our lab uses an online inventory system. If you use the last of a chemical, mark it for reorder immediately.

title: 9  Waste Management
text:
9.1 Biological Waste
Proper waste management is crucial for the safety of our lab members, the university’s facility staff, and the environment.
All biological waste must be decontaminated before final disposal.

title: 9  Waste Management
text:
Solid Biohazard Waste: Dispose of in red biohazard bags. Do not overfill (max 2/3 full). Red bags must be autoclaved before disposal in regular trash.
Liquid Biohazard Waste: Treat with a final concentration of 10% bleach for 30 minutes before pouring down the drain with plenty of water.

title: 9  Waste Management
text:
9.2 Chemical Waste
Chemical waste must be collected in compatible containers and disposed of through the university’s environmental health and safety (EHS) office.

Collection: Use designated, labeled waste containers. Never mix incompatible wastes (e.g., flammables and oxidizers).
Labelling: Each waste container must have a university-approved waste tag listing all components and their approximate concentrations.
Storage: Keep waste containers closed at all times, except when adding waste. Store in a secondary containment tray.

title: 9  Waste Management
text:
9.3 Sharps Waste

Sharps Containers: Dispose of all needles, scalpels, and other sharp objects in puncture-resistant, labeled sharps containers.
Never Recap Needles: Dispose of needles immediately after use without recapping.
Broken Glass: Use a designated “Broken Glass” box for non-contaminated broken glass. If the glass is contaminated with biological or chemical hazards, treat it appropriately before disposal.

title: 9  Waste Management
text:
9.4 Regular Trash

No Hazards: Ensure that no biological, chemical, or sharps materials end up in the regular trash or recycling bins.
Cleanliness: Keep the trash areas tidy and do not block access to waste containers.







ImportantWaste Collection



Contact the Lab Manager when waste containers are 3/4 full to schedule a pickup by EHS.

title: 10  Git Fundamentals
text:
10.1 1. Installation
Git is a version control system that tracks changes to your files. This tutorial will get you comfortable with the essential Git commands used in the S3Bio lab.
Before you can use Git, you need to install it on your machine.

title: 10  Git Fundamentals
text:
WindowsmacOSLinux



Download the Git for Windows installer from git-scm.com.
Run the installer and follow the prompts. We recommend the default settings unless you have specific requirements.
This will also install Git Bash, a terminal that provides a Linux-like environment for running Git commands.



The easiest way to install Git on macOS is via Homebrew:
brew install git
Alternatively, you can install it by running any Git command (like git --version) in the Terminal, which will prompt you to install the Xcode Command Line Tools.


On Debian-based systems (like Ubuntu), use apt:
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install git
On Fedora/Red Hat-based systems, use dnf:
sudo dnf install git

title: 10  Git Fundamentals
text:
10.2 Setting Up Git
First, configure your name and email. This information will be attached to every commit you make.
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"

title: 10  Git Fundamentals
text:
10.3 Basic Workflow
The core Git workflow consists of three steps: Edit, Stage, and Commit.

10.3.1 Initializing a Repository
To start tracking a new project:
cd my-project
git init


10.3.2 Tracking Changes
To see the status of your files:
git status
To stage a file for a commit:
git add filename.txt
# Or stage everything
git add .


10.3.3 Committing Changes
To save your staged changes to the repository history:
git commit -m "feat: add initial analysis script"

title: 10  Git Fundamentals
text:
10.4 Reviewing History
To see a list of all commits in your repository:
git log --oneline --graph --decorate

title: 10  Git Fundamentals
text:
10.5 Undoing Changes
If you’ve made a mistake, you can discard changes to a file that haven’t been staged yet:
git checkout -- filename.txt






TipLearn More



For a deeper dive into Git commands, we recommend the Pro Git Book.

title: 11  GitHub Collaboration
text:
11.1 1. Remote Repositories
GitHub is a hosting service for Git repositories that makes it easy to collaborate with other lab members.
A remote is a version of your project that is hosted on the internet (like GitHub).

title: 11  GitHub Collaboration
text:
11.1.1 Cloning a Repository
To download a repository from the S3Bio organization:
git clone https://github.com/S3Bio/repo-name.git


11.1.2 Pushing Changes
To upload your local commits to GitHub:
git push origin main
# Replace 'main' with your branch name (e.g., 'feature/new-analysis')


11.1.3 Pulling Changes
To update your local repository with changes from GitHub:
git pull origin main

title: 11  GitHub Collaboration
text:
11.2 2. Forking and Pull Requests (PRs)
If you don’t have write access to a repository, you can fork it, which creates a personal copy on your GitHub account.

Fork the repository on GitHub.
Clone your fork locally.
Make changes and push them to your fork.
Open a Pull Request on the original repository to propose your changes.

title: 11  GitHub Collaboration
text:
11.3 3. Resolving Merge Conflicts
A merge conflict happens when two people change the same part of a file in different ways.

Git will mark the conflict in the file: text     <<<<<<< HEAD     Changes in your current branch     =======     Changes from the other branch     >>>>>>> branch-name
Manually edit the file to choose the correct version.
Stage the resolved file: git add filename.txt.
Commit the resolution: git commit.

title: 11  GitHub Collaboration
text:
11.4 4. Issues and Collaboration
Use GitHub Issues to report bugs, request features, or discuss project ideas. Tag your teammates using their @username to notify them.






NoteLab Rules



Always refer to our GitHub Workflow & Best Practices for the lab’s specific rules on branching and code reviews.

title: 12  GitHub Workflow & Best Practices
text:
12.1 Our Workflow: The Feature Branch Model
The S3Bio lab uses GitHub for version control, collaboration, and project management. Following a consistent workflow ensures that our research is reproducible and our codebase is maintainable.
We follow a standard feature branch workflow to keep our main branch stable.

title: 12  GitHub Workflow & Best Practices
text:
Create a Branch: Never work directly on main. Create a descriptive branch name (e.g., feature/rna-seq-analysis or bugfix/fix-plotting-error).
Commit Often: Make small, frequent commits with clear messages.
Open a Pull Request (PR): Once your work is ready (or even while it’s in progress), open a PR to merge into main.
Code Review: At least one other lab member must review and approve your PR before it can be merged.
Merge and Delete: After approval and successful CI checks, merge the PR and delete the feature branch.

title: 12  GitHub Workflow & Best Practices
text:
12.2 Commit Message Conventions
Good commit messages make it easier to track changes. We recommend the following format:
[Type]: Short description (max 50 chars)
Common types: - feat: A new feature or analysis. - fix: A bug fix. - docs: Documentation changes. - refactor: Code changes that neither fix a bug nor add a feature. - data: Adding or updating small data files.

title: 12  GitHub Workflow & Best Practices
text:
12.3 Repository Structure
To keep our projects organized, please follow this general directory structure:
project-name/
├── data/           # Raw and processed data (see note below)
├── docs/           # Project-specific documentation
├── results/        # Output plots, tables, and reports
├── src/            # Source code (R, Python, etc.)
├── README.md       # Project overview and instructions
└── .gitignore      # Files to exclude from version control

title: 12  GitHub Workflow & Best Practices
text:
12.4 Best Practices






ImportantSecurity First



NEVER commit sensitive information such as API keys, passwords, or private laboratory credentials. Use .env files and ensure they are listed in your .gitignore.



Data Management: Avoid committing large datasets (>50MB). Use our lab’s shared drive or specialized data repositories for large files, and include a script in src/ to download or process them.
Reproducibility: Ensure your code is well-commented and includes a requirements.txt or environment.yml file.
README: Every repository should have a README.md that explains the project’s purpose, how to install dependencies, and how to run the analysis.
Issues: Use GitHub Issues to track tasks, bugs, and feature requests.

title: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management
text:
13.1 Why a Personal Study Repository?
While the S3Bio GitHub organization is for official lab projects, we highly recommend that every student and researcher maintains a personal GitHub repository for study planning, personal documentation, and tracking their research journey.
A personal repository acts as your “digital lab notebook” and “career portfolio.”
crumbs: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management

title: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management
text:
Plan & Track: Use GitHub Issues and Projects to plan your weekly tasks and long-term milestones.
Consolidate: Keep your study notes, literature reviews, and personal learning resources in one place.
Reflect: Tracking your results and observations over time helps you see your progress and refine your methods.
crumbs: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management

title: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management
text:
13.2 Best Practice Structure
We recommend a structure similar to this for your personal research/study repo:
research-journal/
├── planning/          # Weekly plans, meeting notes, project proposals
├── notes/             # Literature reviews, course notes, technique summaries
├── scripts/           # Personal helper scripts or learning exercises
├── results-archive/   # Summaries of your key findings (not raw data)
└── README.md          # Overview of your research interests and current goals
crumbs: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management

title: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management
text:
13.3 Study Planning with GitHub Tools

13.3.1 Using Issues for Tasks
Treat every task (e.g., “Read Paper X,” “Run Simulation Y”) as a GitHub Issue. This allows you to: - Assign labels (e.g., Priority: High, Category: Reading). - Keep a history of your thought process in the comments. - Link issues to your code commits.


13.3.2 Using Projects for Milestones
Use a GitHub Project (Kanban board) to visualize your progress across To Do, In Progress, and Done columns.
crumbs: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management

title: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management
text:
13.4 Keeping Results and Data






WarningData Security Rule



Never commit large, sensitive, or raw datasets to your personal repository. Use the lab’s shared drive or official repositories for these.



Summaries Only: Your personal repo should contain summaries (plots, key tables, observations) rather than raw data.
Links: Store links to the official lab datasets in your planning documents to maintain a connection between your notes and the source of truth.
crumbs: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management

title: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management
text:
13.5 Privacy and Sharing

Public vs. Private: You can keep your study repo private, but we encourage making sections of it public to build your professional profile.
Collaboration: You can invite your advisor as a collaborator to your private repo for more direct feedback on your planning and notes.







TipLab Requirement



During your monthly check-in, be prepared to share your recent planning and study notes from your repository. This helps your advisor provide better support for your learning and research.
crumbs: 13  Personal GitHub Repositories for Study Management

title: 14  GitHub Project Management: Issues & Projects
text:
14.1 Using GitHub Issues for Tasks
In the S3Bio lab, we use GitHub’s built-in project management tools to organize our work, whether for individual study plans or collaborative package development.
An Issue is a single, actionable unit of work.
crumbs: 14  GitHub Project Management: Issues & Projects

title: 14  GitHub Project Management: Issues & Projects
text:
14.1.1 For Study Management
Treat every study-related task as an issue in your personal repository.

Title: Clear and concise (e.g., “Read & summarize Smith (2024) paper”).
Description: Detailed notes, checkboxes for sub-tasks, and links to relevant files.
Labels: Use labels like Priority: High, Topic: Modelling, or Status: To Read.
Comments: Use comments to record your thoughts, questions, and progress.



14.1.2 For Package Development
Issues are the standard way to track bugs, features, and improvements.

Templates: Use issue templates (Bug Report, Feature Request) to ensure all necessary information is provided.
References: Link issues to specific lines of code or other issues using their ID (e.g., #42).
Milestones: Assign issues to a specific Milestone to track progress towards a release.
crumbs: 14  GitHub Project Management: Issues & Projects

title: 14  GitHub Project Management: Issues & Projects
text:
14.2 Using GitHub Projects for Milestones
A Project is a high-level view that allows you to manage and visualize multiple issues.

14.2.1 Setting Up a Project
We recommend using the Table or Board (Kanban) view.

Board View: Organizes issues into columns like To Do, In Progress, and Done. This is ideal for tracking day-to-day progress.
Table View: Useful for a more detailed, spreadsheet-like view of all tasks and their metadata.



14.2.2 Project Milestones and Goals

Personal Study: Create a Project for each semester or major research milestone (e.g., “MSc Thesis - Phase 1”).
Package Development: Use Projects to manage a new feature release or a version update (e.g., “MyPackage.jl v2.0”).
crumbs: 14  GitHub Project Management: Issues & Projects

title: 14  GitHub Project Management: Issues & Projects
text:
14.3 Best Practices & Lab Rules






ImportantLab Requirement



All tasks and bugs for official lab packages must be recorded as GitHub Issues. This ensures that the history of the package’s development is transparent and documented.



Keep it Actionable: Every issue should have a clear “definition of done.”
Close Issues Promptly: Once a task is complete or a bug is fixed, close the issue and link to the relevant commit or PR.
Regular Reviews: During your weekly or monthly meetings with your advisor, use your GitHub Project board as the primary tool for discussing your progress and future plans.







TipLearn More




GitHub Issues Documentation
GitHub Projects Documentation

title: 15  Quarto Basics
text:
15.1 Installation
Quarto is the primary tool we use in the S3Bio lab for documenting our research, performing data analysis, and creating reports. It allows us to combine text, code, and results into a single, professional document.
Before using Quarto, you need to install it on your system.

title: 15  Quarto Basics
text:
WindowsmacOSLinux



Download the latest Windows MSI installer from the Quarto Download page.
Run the installer and follow the instructions.
Verify the installation by opening a terminal (PowerShell or Git Bash) and running: bash  quarto --version



The easiest way to install Quarto on macOS is via Homebrew:
brew install --cask quarto
Alternatively, you can download the .pkg installer from the Quarto website.


On Debian-based systems (like Ubuntu), download the .deb file and install it:
# Example for version 1.4.549
sudo gdebi quarto-1.4.549-linux-amd64.deb
For other distributions, you can download the .tar.gz file and extract it to your desired location.

title: 15  Quarto Basics
section: 15.2 The Anatomy of a Quarto Document
text:
15.2 The Anatomy of a Quarto Document
A .qmd file consists of three main parts:

YAML Header: Contained between --- at the top of the file. It defines the document’s title, author, output format, and other metadata.
---
title: "My Analysis"
author: "S3Bio Lab Member"
format: html
engine: julia
---
Markdown Text: The narrative part of your document, where you explain your methods and interpret your results.
Code Cells: Blocks of code (R, Python, or Julia) that perform your analysis and generate outputs like plots and tables.

title: 15  Quarto Basics
text:
15.3 Markdown Basics
The narrative part of your document is written in Markdown. Here are some commonly used commands:



Feature

title: 15  Quarto Basics
text:
15.4 Code Cells
To add a code cell, use triple backticks followed by the language in curly braces:
```{julia}
#| label: example-plot
#| fig-cap: "An example plot in Julia"
using Plots
x = 1:10; y = rand(10);
plot(x, y, title="S3Bio Lab Example")
```
The #| lines are cell options that control how the code and its output are displayed.

title: 15  Quarto Basics
text:
15.5 Rendering Documents
To “render” your .qmd file into its final format (HTML, PDF, or Word), use the Render button in your IDE (like RStudio or VS Code) or the command line:
quarto render my-document.qmd

title: 15  Quarto Basics
text:
15.6 Why We Use Quarto

Reproducibility: The results are generated directly from the code.
Transparency: Your analysis logic is clear and well-documented.
Flexibility: One document can be rendered into multiple formats.







TipResources



Check out the official Quarto documentation for a comprehensive guide.

title: 16  Julia Programming
text:
16.1 Installation
Julia is the primary language for numerical analysis and simulation in the S3Bio lab. Its “high-level” syntax combined with “low-level” performance makes it ideal for systems biology.
We recommend using juliaup, the official Julia installer and version multiplexer. It makes it easy to install and update different versions of Julia.
After installation, verify it by running julia in your terminal.

title: 16  Julia Programming
text:
WindowsmacOSLinux


Open a terminal (PowerShell or Command Prompt) and run:
winget install julia -s msstore


Use Homebrew to install juliaup:
brew install juliaup


Run the following command in your shell:
curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh

title: 16  Julia Programming
text:
16.2 Working Directory & Environment Best Practices
In our lab, every project must have its own isolated environment. This ensures that your code remains reproducible even as packages are updated globally.

16.2.1 Project Activation
Always start your Julia session by activating the local environment.
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
Alternatively, start Julia with the --project flag:
julia --project


16.2.2 Dependency Management

Project.toml: Lists the packages your project depends on.
Manifest.toml: Records the exact versions of every dependency (including sub-dependencies).

Lab Rule: Always commit both Project.toml and Manifest.toml to your Git repository.






TipLearn More




Official Julia Documentation
Modern Julia Workflows

title: 17  Julia for Data Analysis
text:
17.1 Data Collection & Import
In the S3Bio lab, our data analysis workflow is a systematic process built on the JuliaStats and Tidier.jl ecosystems. This chapter breaks down our best practices across the five core stages of research analysis.
We use TidierFiles.jl for a Tidyverse-consistent data import experience.

title: 17  Julia for Data Analysis
text:
17.1.1 Best Practices

Standardized Inputs: Prefer CSV or Arrow formats for tabular data.
Remote Data: If your data is hosted online, use download() before reading.
Lab Rule: Always read data as a DataFrame to ensure compatibility with our Tidy tools.

using Tidier, StatsKit

# Importing from a local CSV
df_raw = read_csv("data/raw_experiment_data.csv")

title: 17  Julia for Data Analysis
text:
17.2 Data Preprocessing & Cleaning
Data cleaning is the most critical step for reproducibility. We use TidierData.jl to create clear, auditable cleaning pipelines.

17.2.1 Best Practices

Handle Missing Values: Explicitly deal with missing values using @filter(!ismissing(col)) or imputation.
Type Conversion: Ensure columns have correct types (e.g., categorical for genotypes).
Normalization: Perform all scaling and normalization within the cleaning pipeline.

df_clean = @chain df_raw begin
    @filter(!ismissing(quality))
    @mutate(genotype = categorical(genotype))
    @mutate(value_norm = (value - mean(value)) / std(value))
end

title: 17  Julia for Data Analysis
text:
17.3 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
EDA allows us to understand the distributions and relationships in our data before formal modeling.

17.3.1 Best Practices

Summarization: Use @group_by and @summarize to calculate key metrics.
Quick Visualization: Use TidierPlots.jl to spot outliers or trends.

# Summarizing by group
summary_stats = @chain df_clean begin
    @group_by(genotype, treatment)
    @summarize(mean_val = mean(value_norm), n = n())
end

# Quick EDA plot
df_clean |>
    ggplot(aes(x = :value_norm, fill = :genotype)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.5)

title: 17  Julia for Data Analysis
text:
17.4 Statistical Analysis
For formal hypothesis testing and modeling, we transition to the robust JuliaStats ecosystem, primarily GLM.jl and MixedModels.jl.

17.4.1 Best Practices

Model Choice: Use lm() for simple linear models and lme() for mixed-effects models (when you have biological replicates).
Inference: Always report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not just p-values.

# Fitting a Linear Model
model = lm(@formula(value_norm ~ genotype * treatment), df_clean)

# Inspecting results
println(coeftable(model))
println("R²: ", r2(model))

title: 17  Julia for Data Analysis
text:
17.5 Data Presentation
Presentation-quality figures and tables are the final output of our workflow.

17.5.1 Best Practices

Layered Graphics: Build complex plots layer-by-layer using TidierPlots.jl.
Theming: Use consistent themes (e.g., theme_minimal()) and lab-standard color palettes.
Exporting: Save figures as vector graphics (.pdf or .svg) for publication.

final_plot = df_clean |>
    ggplot(aes(x = :genotype, y = :value_norm, color = :treatment)) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier_shape = NA) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) +
    labs(
        title = "Impact of Treatment across Genotypes",
        subtitle = "n = 3 biological replicates",
        x = "Genotype",
        y = "Normalized Expression (Z-score)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

# Save for publication
# ggsave("results/figure1.svg", final_plot)

title: 17  Julia for Data Analysis
text:
17.6 Compliance with Reproducible Research Rules
To ensure your Julia analysis is fully reproducible and compliant with Lab Rules, you must follow these technical requirements:

Environment Lockdown: Always include Project.toml and Manifest.toml. This ensures that anyone else can run your analysis with the exact same package versions.
No Absolute Paths: Use the data/ directory relative to your project root. Never use paths like C:/Users/....
Scripted Analysis: Every result must be generated by code within your Quarto document. Avoid “manual” steps in the REPL that are not recorded in the script.
Seed for Randomness: If your analysis involves random sampling or simulations, always set a seed using Random.seed!(123) for deterministic results.
Version Control: Commit your .qmd files and helper scripts to GitHub. Do not commit large datasets (use the lab’s shared drive instead).







TipLearn More

title: 18  Reproducible Research Rules
text:
18.1 Lab Rule 1: No “Shadow” Data or Results
In the S3Bio lab, reproducibility is not just a goal; it’s a requirement. We use Quarto to ensure that every result, plot, and table in our publications can be independently verified and recreated.
All data analysis must be performed in a Quarto (.qmd) document. Never copy and paste numbers or plots from an interactive session into a report. The code that generated the result must be present in the document.

title: 18  Reproducible Research Rules
text:
18.2 Lab Rule 2: Self-Contained Projects
Every project must be self-contained. This means:

Data: Small datasets should be in a data/ folder.
Dependencies: Include Project.toml and Manifest.toml files to specify the exact versions of the Julia packages used.
Paths: Always use relative paths (e.g., data/samples.csv), never absolute paths (e.g., C:/Users/name/Desktop/data.csv).

title: 18  Reproducible Research Rules
text:
18.3 Lab Rule 3: Use Version Control (Git/GitHub)
Every Quarto project must be tracked in a Git repository and hosted on the S3Bio GitHub organization. This allows us to see how the analysis has evolved and to revert to previous versions if necessary.

title: 18  Reproducible Research Rules
text:
18.4 Lab Rule 4: Clear Documentation
Your Quarto documents should not just be blocks of code. Use Markdown to explain the why and how of your analysis. This is essential for someone (including your future self) to understand and reproduce your results. Use Markdown to:

State the objective of the analysis.
Describe the methods and any assumptions made.
Explain the findings and how they relate to the project’s goals.

title: 18  Reproducible Research Rules
text:
18.5 Lab Rule 5: Regular Rendering
Render your documents frequently to ensure they still work. A Quarto document that doesn’t render is a broken analysis. Use quarto preview during development to see changes in real-time.

title: 18  Reproducible Research Rules
text:
18.6 Lab Rule 6: Quarto for Communication
All internal lab reports, presentations, and supplementary materials for publications must be created using Quarto. This ensures that the “source of truth” is always the code and that any changes to the data are automatically reflected in all communication materials.






ImportantReproducibility Checklist



Before sharing your analysis with the lab, ask yourself: 1. Does it render from start to finish on another machine using quarto render? 2. Are all data sources and dependencies clearly defined? 3. Is the logic of the analysis explained in the text? 4. Are all figures and tables generated directly from the code?

title: 18  Reproducible Research Rules
text:
18.7 Example: A Reproducible Project Structure
my-reproducible-project/
├── data/           # Raw and cleaned data
├── docs/           # Project-specific documentation
├── results/        # Rendered HTML/PDF reports
├── src/            # Helper scripts (.jl)
├── README.md       # Project overview
├── analysis.qmd    # The main Quarto analysis file
├── Project.toml    # Julia project dependencies
└── Manifest.toml   # Precise Julia package versions

title: 19  Package Structure & PkgTemplates
text:
19.1 Creating a Package with PkgTemplates.jl
In the S3Bio lab, we use PkgTemplates.jl to ensure that all new packages follow a consistent structure and include necessary files for testing, documentation, and continuous integration.

title: 19  Package Structure & PkgTemplates
text:
19.1.1 Installation
Add the template generator to your global environment:
using Pkg
Pkg.add("PkgTemplates")


19.1.2 Generating a New Package
We recommend using the following template configuration for lab projects:
using PkgTemplates

tpl = Template(;
    user="S3Bio",                      # GitHub organization
    authors="S3Bio Lab Member",        # Your name
    dir=".",                           # Directory to create the package in
    plugins=[
        License(; name="MIT"),         # Choose the appropriate license
        Git(; branch="main"),          # Default branch
        GitHubActions(),               # Continuous Integration
        Codecov(),                     # Code coverage
        Documenter{GitHubActions}(),   # Auto-generate documentation
    ],
)

tpl("MyNewProject")

title: 19  Package Structure & PkgTemplates
text:
19.2 Standard Package Anatomy
A well-structured Julia package generated by our template looks like this:
MyPackage/
├── src/
│   └── MyPackage.jl  # Main module file
├── test/
│   └── runtests.jl   # Test suite
├── docs/             # Documentation source (Markdown)
├── Project.toml      # Package metadata and dependencies
├── Manifest.toml     # Exact dependency versions
└── README.md         # Project overview and usage

19.2.1 Key Files

src/: All your source code goes here. The main entry point is MyPackage.jl.
Project.toml: Defines the package name, UUID, and its dependencies.
Manifest.toml: Lock file that ensures reproducibility by recording the exact versions of all dependencies.

title: 20  Development Workflow & Revise.jl
text:
20.1 Setting Up Revise.jl
A productive Julia development workflow is interactive. In the S3Bio lab, we use Revise.jl as a mandatory tool to enable rapid code modification without needing to restart the Julia REPL.
Revise should be installed in your global environment and automatically loaded when you start Julia.

title: 20  Development Workflow & Revise.jl
text:
20.1.1 Installation
In the Julia REPL, press ] to enter Pkg mode:
pkg> add Revise


20.1.2 Configure Automatic Loading
Create (or edit) your ~/.julia/config/startup.jl file and add the following lines:
try
    using Revise
catch e
    @warn "Error loading Revise" e
end

title: 20  Development Workflow & Revise.jl
text:
20.2 Interactive Development Workflow
The typical workflow for modifying a package in the lab is as follows:

Open Julia in your project directory: julia --project.
Load your package: using MyPackage.
Use Revise: Any changes you make to the source code files in src/ will be immediately reflected in your current Julia session.
No Restart Required: You can keep your session open for days while you iterate on your code and analysis.

title: 20  Development Workflow & Revise.jl
text:
20.3 Project Activation
Always ensure you are working within the correct project environment.

REPL: Use Pkg.activate(".") if you didn’t start with the --project flag.
VS Code: The Julia extension automatically detects and activates your project environment if configured correctly.

title: 21  Testing & Continuous Integration
text:
21.1 Writing Unit Tests
Testing is fundamental to ensuring the correctness and stability of our research software. In the S3Bio lab, all packages must follow a rigorous testing and CI protocol.
We use the built-in Test standard library to write unit tests for all our functions.

title: 21  Testing & Continuous Integration
21  Testing & Continuous Integration
text:
21.2 Running Tests Locally
To run your tests from the Julia REPL:
using Pkg
Pkg.test()
This will automatically create a temporary environment and run your tests in it.

title: 21  Testing & Continuous Integration
text:
21.3 GitHub Actions (CI)
Our packages are automatically tested on every push and pull request via GitHub Actions. Our templates (from PkgTemplates.jl) automatically configure this for you.

21.3.1 CI Requirements

Passed Builds: Every PR must pass all CI checks (Linux, macOS, Windows) for the supported Julia versions.
Code Coverage: We use Codecov to track our test coverage.

Minimum Requirement: All lab packages must maintain at least 80% code coverage.








ImportantLab Rule



A pull request will not be merged until it passes all CI checks and meets the code coverage requirements.

title: 21  Testing & Continuous Integration
text:
21.4 Troubleshooting CI
If your CI build fails, check the GitHub Actions logs to identify the error. Often, it’s due to a missing dependency in Project.toml or a platform-specific issue.

title: 22  Package Publishing & Documentation
text:
22.1 Documenting Your Package
The final stage of package development in the S3Bio lab is documentation and publishing.
We use Documenter.jl to create professional, Markdown-based documentation.

title: 22  Package Publishing & Documentation
text:
22.1.1 Why Documentation?

It explains the theory behind your code.
It provides examples and tutorials for other users.
It automatically generates a reference guide from your docstrings.



22.1.2 Documentation Structure
Your documentation lives in the docs/ folder:
docs/
├── make.jl    # Build script
└── src/
    └── index.md # Main documentation page


22.1.3 Auto-Deployment
Our templates configure GitHub Actions to automatically build and deploy your documentation to GitHub Pages whenever you push to the main branch.

title: 22  Package Publishing & Documentation
text:
22.2 Registering Your Package
Most of our lab packages are private or shared within our GitHub organization. For general-purpose tools, we may register them in the General Julia registry.

22.2.1 Registration Process

Tag a Release: Use a Git tag (e.g., v1.0.0) to mark your release.
Use JuliaRegistrator: We use the Registrator bot on GitHub. Comment @JuliaRegistrator register on a commit or PR to start the process.
Lab Approval: Consult with the PI before registering any package in a public registry.

title: 22  Package Publishing & Documentation
text:
22.3 Best Practices for Maintenance

Semantic Versioning (SemVer): Follow SemVer (e.g., v1.2.3). Increase the major version for breaking changes.
Release Notes: Maintain a CHANGELOG.md to track changes between versions.
Dependency Updates: Periodically update your Project.toml and Manifest.toml to use the latest versions of your dependencies.
